newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian copper industry wants higher import duties.
newsitem.headline: Indian copper industry wants higher import duties.

text.p: India's copper industry on Sunday demanded higher duties on imports of finished goods which are threatening domestic manufacturers.

Bombay Metal Exchange (BME) President Sharad Parikh said a uniform import tariff on copper raw materials and finished products had badly affected domestic producers and trade. The BME represents both the industry and traders.

"Many domestic copper product manufacturing companies have cut back production by as much as 50 to 60 percent and some have closed down," Parikh told Reuters. "What we are demanding is that the differential in duties imposed on copper raw materials and finished goods be at least 15 percent."
Parikh said Indian producers of copper products had been facing unfair competition from imports due to the uniform tariff on raw materials and semi-finished goods.
The import duty on copper raw materials such as wire bars, cathodes, cakes, billets and scrap is 30 percent, which is the same as on finished goods like sheets, pipes, strips, rods and wires.
Parikh said industrial users of copper were directly importing finished products instead of buying them from domestic units, whose costs of production were high.
"This is because we are still dependent on imported raw materials which are converted into finished products," he said.

The BME has, in a memorandum sent to Finance Minister P. Chidambaram last week and made available to Reuters on Sunday, cited high interest rates and local taxes as the other factors which inflated domestic production costs.
It said Indian industrial units borrowed funds from banks at an interest rate of 18 percent while their counterparts abroad got money as cheap as 7-8 percent.
The memorandum said the foreign producers were also not subject to sales tax, entry tax, turnover tax and excise which made their products cheaper.
"This (the uniform tariff) is not fair to downstream producing units in India," it added.

Chidambaram had in the fiscal budget for 1996/97 (April/March) removed an existing 10 percent differential in import duties on copper raw materials and semi-finished goods in line with India's economic reforms.
Analysts said India's sluggish industrial growth had also affected copper raw material producers such as state-owned Hindustan Copper Ltd (HCL).
HCL's copper cathode production fell steeply to 14,251 tonnes in September 1996 from 19,970 tonnes in the corresponding month a year ago.
